metadata.title: Programming Variables
metadata.purpose: Defines all training variables Claude uses to build and progress TRAIN programs. Every set, rep, tempo, rest period, and progression decision references this file.
metadata.credit: Draft foundation by Johnny — expanded for Claude integration

instructions_for_claude.step_1: Identify client goal from client_program_goals.json — this sets the base variable ranges
instructions_for_claude.step_2: Apply experience level modifier from client_assessment_schema.json
instructions_for_claude.step_3: Apply recovery modifier (sleep + stress + recent_frequency from onboarding)
instructions_for_claude.step_4: Select rep range, sets, tempo, and rest from the goal-specific presets below
instructions_for_claude.step_5: Assign session position (Primary / Accessory / Finisher) to determine variable tier
instructions_for_claude.step_6: Build week-over-week progression using the progressive_overload section
instructions_for_claude.step_7: Schedule deload using deload_protocols — default every 4th week

volume.definition: Total training stimulus — the combination of sets, reps, and load that drives adaptation.

sets.definition: Number of working sets per exercise, excluding warm-up sets

by_goal.fat_loss: 2–3 sets per exercise — higher exercise variety, lower per-exercise volume
by_goal.muscle_gain: 3–5 sets per exercise — higher per-exercise volume for hypertrophy stimulus
by_goal.performance: 3–5 sets — heavier load, full recovery between sets

by_experience.beginner: 2–3 sets — adaptation comes from frequency, not volume
by_experience.intermediate: 3–4 sets — can handle increased per-exercise volume
by_experience.advanced: 4–5 sets — requires high volume to drive further adaptation

sets.warm_up_sets: Always include 1–2 progressive warm-up sets before working sets on primary compound movements. These do not count toward working set total.

reps.definition: Number of repetitions per set — determines the training stimulus (strength, hypertrophy, or endurance)

strength.use_for: Performance and Strength & Power goals. Advanced clients only.

hypertrophy_heavy.stimulus: Mechanical tension — primary driver of muscle growth

hypertrophy_moderate.use_for: Most goals — the universal hypertrophy range

hypertrophy_high.use_for: Fat loss, accessory work, isolation finishers

endurance.use_for: General health finishers, active recovery, corrective work

weekly_volume_per_muscle_group.definition: Total number of hard sets per muscle group per week — the primary driver of hypertrophy over time

minimum_effective_volume.large_muscle_groups: 10 sets per week (back, chest, quads, glutes)
minimum_effective_volume.small_muscle_groups: 6 sets per week (biceps, triceps, calves, rear delts)

maximum_adaptive_volume.large_muscle_groups: 20 sets per week — beyond this, recovery suffers

by_goal.fat_loss: 10–14 sets per large muscle group — enough to preserve muscle
by_goal.muscle_gain: 14–20 sets per large muscle group — push volume progressively

by_experience.beginner: Start at minimum effective volume. Add volume only after 3–4 weeks of consistency.
by_experience.intermediate: Mid-range. Progress volume week over week within the mesocycle.
by_experience.advanced: Upper range. Requires careful deload programming to avoid overtraining.

weekly_volume_per_muscle_group.coaching_note: Track weekly sets per muscle group in the program. If a muscle is appearing less than minimum effective volume, add an accessory exercise or increase sets.

intensity.definition: How hard each set is — expressed as absolute load, RPE, or RIR. The primary driver of strength adaptation.

load.definition: The absolute weight used — expressed as percentage of 1 Rep Max (1RM) or as a practical descriptor

practical_descriptors.light: Could do many more reps — RPE 5–6
practical_descriptors.moderate: Challenging but form is solid — RPE 7
practical_descriptors.heavy: Hard, 1–3 reps left in the tank — RPE 8–9
practical_descriptors.maximal: Near failure or at failure — RPE 9–10

by_goal_default.fat_loss: Light to moderate — preserve muscle without taxing recovery
by_goal_default.muscle_gain: Moderate to heavy — mechanical tension drives growth
by_goal_default.performance: Heavy to maximal on primary lifts
by_goal_default.general_health: Light to moderate — sustainability over intensity

RPE.name: Rate of Perceived Exertion
RPE.definition: How hard a set feels — 10 is absolute maximum effort, 1 is no effort

guide.RPE_5: Very easy. Could do 5+ more reps. Warm-up territory.
guide.RPE_7: Moderate. 3 reps left in the tank. This is the minimum for a productive working set.
guide.RPE_8: Hard. 2 reps left. Most working sets should land here.
guide.RPE_9: Very hard. 1 rep left. Primary compound heavy sets.
guide.RPE_10: Max effort. Nothing left. Use rarely — 1RM testing or true failure sets only.

RPE.coaching_note: RPE is the most practical intensity tool for most clients. Teach it early — ask 'how many more reps could you have done?' after every set.

RIR.name: Reps in Reserve
RIR.definition: The number of reps a client could have done before reaching failure — the inverse of RPE

guide.RIR_4_plus: Too easy. Increase load or reps.
guide.RIR_3: Moderate. Acceptable for warm-up or deload sets.
guide.RIR_2: Good working set intensity. Most accessory work lives here.
guide.RIR_0: Failure. Use sparingly — isolation finishers only.

RIR.progression_trigger: When a client consistently hits RIR 3+ on their working sets, increase load by the minimum increment (2.5–5 lbs).
RIR.coaching_note: RIR is often easier for beginners to understand than RPE — 'how many more could you do?' is a more concrete question than 'how hard was that on a scale of 10?'

tempo.definition: The speed of each phase of a movement — written as a 4-number code: Eccentric–Pause–Concentric–Reset

standard.description: 2 seconds down, no pause, 2 seconds up, no pause at top
standard.use_for: Most working sets — basic tempo control

hypertrophy.description: 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at bottom, 2 seconds up
hypertrophy.use_for: Muscle gain primary goal — maximizes time under tension

eccentric_focus.description: 4 second slow lowering, 1 second pause, 2 seconds up
eccentric_focus.use_for: Advanced hypertrophy — eccentric overload drives significant muscle damage and growth

pause_rep.description: 2 seconds down, 2 second dead-stop pause, 2 seconds up
pause_rep.use_for: Eliminating stretch-reflex, building strength from dead positions, squat and bench

explosive.description: 2 seconds down, no pause, explosive concentric
explosive.use_for: Power and performance — Olympic movements, jumps, throws

controlled.description: 2 seconds down, 1 pause bottom, 2 seconds up, 1 pause top
controlled.use_for: Beginners learning movement patterns — slows everything down for technique

by_goal_default.general_health: 2-1-2-0 — controlled throughout for safety and awareness

tempo.coaching_note: Never assign tempo to beginners in the first 2 weeks — focus on learning the pattern. Introduce tempo once the movement is solid. The eccentric phase is where the most muscle damage (and therefore growth) occurs — always cue clients to control the lowering phase.

rest.definition: Recovery time between sets — determines readiness for the next set and influences the training stimulus

fat_loss.note: Shorter rest increases metabolic demand and caloric burn

muscle_gain.note: Longer rest allows full CNS recovery for maximum mechanical tension

performance.note: Power and strength require full recovery to maintain output quality

general_health.note: Standard rest — enough to recover, not so long the session drags

rest.between_exercises: 90–120 seconds when transitioning between different movement patterns. Less when supersetting opposing muscle groups.

superset_rest.antagonist_superset: Rest 30–45 seconds between exercises within the superset. Rest 60–90 seconds after completing both exercises.
superset_rest.same_muscle_superset: No rest between exercises. 90–120 seconds after completing both.

rest.coaching_note: Rest periods are a programming variable — treat them with the same intention as sets and reps. Cutting rest too short on heavy compound sets reduces performance and increases injury risk.

session_structure.definition: How exercises are ordered and grouped within a session — determines efficiency, safety, and stimulus quality

primary.definition: The main compound movements — highest neural demand, done first when energy is fresh
primary.sets_reps_guide: 3–5 sets, 4–8 reps, heavy to moderate load

accessory.definition: Secondary movements supporting the primary — address weak links and add volume

finisher.definition: High-rep isolation or conditioning work — accumulates volume and creates metabolic demand
finisher.sets_reps_guide: 2–3 sets, 12–20+ reps, light to moderate load

superset_pairing.definition: Performing two exercises back-to-back with minimal rest between them

antagonist_superset.definition: Pairing opposing muscle groups — one rests while the other works
antagonist_superset.benefit: Saves time, maintains strength output, increases session density
antagonist_superset.best_for: Fat loss, muscle gain accessory work

compound_superset.definition: Two compound movements for the same muscle group
compound_superset.benefit: Massive volume accumulation — use for advanced clients
compound_superset.caution: Fatiguing — do not use on primary strength movements for beginners

unrelated_superset.definition: Pairing two exercises that don't interfere with each other
unrelated_superset.benefit: Time efficiency — one muscle rests while another works

circuit.definition: 3+ exercises performed consecutively with minimal rest — high metabolic demand
circuit.use_for: Fat loss finishers, general health clients, time-limited sessions
circuit.structure: 3–5 exercises, 12–15 reps each, 30–60 seconds rest after full circuit, repeat 2–4 rounds
circuit.caution: Do not use circuits for primary compound strength work — fatigue compromises form and reduces strength output

progressive_overload.definition: The systematic increase of training demand over time — the single most important principle in programming. Without progression, there is no adaptation.

add_reps.description: Perform more reps with the same weight
add_reps.when: Client hits the top of their rep range at RIR 2+
add_reps.example: Target 3x8. Client hits 3x10 with 2 reps in reserve → add weight next session
add_reps.best_for: Beginners and intermediate — simplest progression method

add_weight.description: Increase load while maintaining rep range

increments.upper_body: 2.5–5 lbs per session or per week
increments.lower_body: 5–10 lbs per session or per week
increments.isolation: 2.5 lbs — small muscles require small jumps

add_weight.when: Client consistently hits rep range top with RIR 2+ across 2 consecutive sessions
add_weight.best_for: Intermediate and advanced on compound movements

add_sets.description: Increase total working sets per exercise or per muscle group
add_sets.when: Client has been at same rep and weight for 2+ weeks with no fatigue issues
add_sets.increment: Add 1 set at a time — never jump more than 1 set per week per exercise
add_sets.best_for: Muscle gain — volume is the primary driver of hypertrophy over time

reduce_rest.description: Decrease rest periods while maintaining load and reps
reduce_rest.when: Client is recovering well and sessions feel too easy
reduce_rest.increment: Reduce by 10–15 seconds at a time
reduce_rest.best_for: Fat loss and general health — increases density and metabolic demand

increase_tempo.description: Slow down the eccentric or add pauses to increase time under tension
increase_tempo.when: Client has mastered standard tempo and needs more challenge without adding weight
increase_tempo.best_for: Muscle gain — excellent intermediate progression before adding load

increase_range_of_motion.description: Gradually increase depth or range as mobility improves
increase_range_of_motion.when: Client was limited by mobility at program start — now capable of fuller range
increase_range_of_motion.example: Elevated heel squat → flat foot squat → ATG squat (over months)
increase_range_of_motion.best_for: All goals — more ROM = more muscle activation = better results

increase_frequency.description: Train a muscle group more times per week
increase_frequency.when: Client has fully recovered from previous sessions and volume ceiling has been reached at current frequency
increase_frequency.increment: Add 1 session per week — never jump from 2x to 4x per week

progression_decision_tree.week_1_to_2: Establish baseline. Do not progress — focus on movement quality and learning the program.
progression_decision_tree.week_3: If RPE is consistently below 7 → increase reps (stay in same set range). If RPE is 7–8 → maintain.
progression_decision_tree.week_4: If rep range top is consistently hit with RIR 2+ → add weight. If not → maintain reps and load.
progression_decision_tree.week_5_to_7: Continue add-reps or add-weight progression every 1–2 weeks based on RIR.
progression_decision_tree.week_8: Deload. Reassess. Begin next mesocycle at slightly higher baseline.

progressive_overload.coaching_note: Progressive overload is non-negotiable. A program that doesn't progress is just exercise — not training. Always track what the client did last session and ensure this session is slightly harder in at least one variable.

deload_protocols.definition: A planned reduction in training volume and/or intensity to allow full recovery and supercompensation — NOT a rest week

frequency.default: Every 4th week (3 weeks accumulation, 1 week deload)
frequency.high_stress_clients: Every 3rd week — if sleep=poor or stress=very_high in onboarding
frequency.advanced_clients: Every 4th–6th week — higher work capacity, slower fatigue accumulation
frequency.beginner_clients: Every 5th–6th week — accumulate fatigue slowly, deload less frequently

volume_deload.description: Reduce sets by 40–50%, maintain load and reps
volume_deload.best_for: Most clients — preserves strength while reducing fatigue

intensity_deload.description: Reduce load by 40–50%, maintain sets and reps
intensity_deload.best_for: Clients with joint fatigue or accumulated soreness

combined_deload.description: Reduce both volume and intensity by 30–40%
combined_deload.best_for: Advanced clients with high accumulated fatigue

deload_protocols.what_deload_is_not: A deload is NOT a rest week. Clients still train — they just train at reduced demand. Complete rest is only appropriate for illness or acute injury.
signs_a_deload_is_needed_early: Performance is declining despite consistent sleep and nutrition
Persistent joint aching or soreness that doesn't resolve within 48 hours
Client reports feeling drained before sessions start
Mood and motivation have dropped significantly
Sleep quality has worsened despite no life changes
deload_protocols.coaching_note: Frame deloads positively — 'This week we recover so the next 3 weeks can be even stronger.' Clients often resist deloads. Remind them: supercompensation happens during recovery, not during training.

frequency.definition: How often a muscle group is trained per week — independent of training days per week

fat_loss.recommended: Each muscle group 2x per week minimum
fat_loss.rationale: Frequency maintains muscle while creating caloric demand across the week

muscle_gain.rationale: Muscle protein synthesis peaks 24–48 hours post-session — training more frequently maximizes total weekly stimulus

performance.recommended: 2–3x per week for primary patterns, 1x for accessory
performance.rationale: Skill and strength acquisition require frequent practice

general_health.recommended: 2x per week per muscle group minimum
general_health.rationale: Consistency builds the habit — frequency over intensity

full_body_3x.best_for: Beginners, fat loss, general health, 3-day schedules
full_body_3x.structure: A/B/A one week, B/A/B the next — alternate movement emphasis

upper_lower_4x.best_for: Intermediate, muscle gain, fat loss, 4-day schedules

push_pull_legs_6x.best_for: Intermediate to advanced, muscle gain, 5–6 day schedules
push_pull_legs_6x.structure: Push / Pull / Legs / Push / Pull / Legs

full_body_2x.best_for: Busy clients, beginners, general health, 2-day schedules
full_body_2x.structure: 2 full body sessions with 48+ hours between

minimum_recovery_between_sessions.same_muscle_group: 48 hours minimum — never train the same muscle group on back-to-back days
minimum_recovery_between_sessions.upper_lower: 24 hours acceptable — upper and lower don't directly compete for recovery
minimum_recovery_between_sessions.exception: Advanced clients with high work capacity may tolerate 24-hour turnaround on same muscle — monitor carefully

variable_presets_by_goal.description: Complete variable packages for each goal — Claude applies these as starting templates, then adjusts per client modifiers

fat_loss_preset.progression: Add reps first, then reduce rest, then add weight

muscle_gain_preset.progression: Add weight when RIR 2+ consistently, then add sets over mesocycle

performance_preset.progression: Linear load progression on primary lifts weekly

general_health_preset.progression: Add reps, then add sets — load progression secondary
